claim: Ezh2 is widely expressed in the dental epithelium, dental follicle, and dental papilla of control mice prior to root development initiation at the newborn stage.
source: We found that Ezh2 is widely expressed in the dental epithelium, dental follicle, and dental papilla of control mice prior to root development initiation at the newborn stage (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1C demonstrating Ezh2 expression pattern.

claim: H3K27Me3 was detectable in a similar pattern to that of Ezh2 in control mice.
source: H3K27Me3 was detectable in a similar pattern to that of Ezh2 in control mice, consistent with Ezh2's execution of a PRC2-dependent function during molar development (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1E showing H3K27Me3 expression pattern.

claim: Ezh2 executes a PRC2-dependent function during molar development.
source: H3K27Me3 was detectable in a similar pattern to that of Ezh2 in control mice, consistent with Ezh2's execution of a PRC2-dependent function during molar development (Figure 1E).
evidence: Inferred from the similar expression patterns of Ezh2 and H3K27Me3, where H3K27Me3 is a known product of PRC2 complex activity.

claim: Osr2-Cre genetically targets the dental mesenchyme and alveolar bone but not the tooth epithelium.
source: Osr2-Cre genetically targets the dental mesenchyme and alveolar bone but not the tooth epithelium
evidence: Based on established knowledge of Osr2-Cre expression pattern.

claim: Ezh2 and H3K27Me3 were undetectable in the molar mesenchyme of Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl mice at the newborn stage.
source: Indeed, Ezh2 and H3K27Me3 were undetectable in the molar mesenchyme of Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl mice at the newborn stage (Figure 1D and F), indicating efficient tissue-specific deletion of Ezh2 in the dental mesenchyme.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figures 1D and 1F showing absence of Ezh2 and H3K27Me3 in mutant mesenchyme.

claim: There were no morphological differences between the crowns of Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl and control molars at the newborn stage.
source: There were no morphological differences between the crowns of Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl and control molars at the newborn stage (Figure 1A–1B), prior to root development.
evidence: Supported by H&E staining shown in Figures 1A-1B.

claim: Tooth crown formation was similar in Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl and control mice at one week of age.
source: Tooth crown formation was similar in Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl and control mice at one week of age (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–1F), indicating that Ezh2 is dispensable for crown patterning.
evidence: Supported by microCT images in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–1F.

claim: Ezh2 is dispensable for crown patterning.
source: Tooth crown formation was similar in Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl and control mice at one week of age (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–1F), indicating that Ezh2 is dispensable for crown patterning.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that crown formation is normal in Ezh2 mutants.

claim: In control mice, at two weeks after birth the root furcation was well formed, resulting in two roots in the mandibular first molars.
source: In control mice, at two weeks after birth the root furcation was well formed, resulting in two roots in the mandibular first molars (Figure 2A–2E).
evidence: Supported by microCT images in Figures 2A-2E showing normal furcation.

claim: Only one root trunk with no furcation was observed in Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl mandibular first molars at two weeks after birth.
source: Interestingly, only one root trunk with no furcation was observed in Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl mandibular first molars (Figure 2F–2J).
evidence: Supported by microCT images in Figures 2F-2J showing absence of furcation.

claim: The absence of furcation persisted in Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl mice at postnatal 4 weeks.
source: The absence of furcation persisted in Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl mice at postnatal 4 weeks (Figure 2P–2T), by which time the tooth root had completed development in the control group (Figure 2K–2O).
evidence: Supported by microCT images in Figures 2P-2T showing continued absence of furcation at 4 weeks.

claim: The alveolar bone underneath the molar was undetectable throughout all developmental stages in Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl mice.
source: Moreover, the alveolar bone underneath the molar was undetectable throughout all developmental stages in Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl mice.
evidence: Based on observations across multiple time points and imaging modalities.

claim: Dspp expression was not affected in Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl mice.
source: Interestingly, Dspp expression was not affected in Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl mice, indicating that loss of Ezh2 in the dental mesenchyme has no effect on odontoblast differentiation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by Dspp staining shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Loss of Ezh2 in the dental mesenchyme has no effect on odontoblast differentiation.
source: Interestingly, Dspp expression was not affected in Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl mice, indicating that loss of Ezh2 in the dental mesenchyme has no effect on odontoblast differentiation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Inferred from normal Dspp expression, which is a marker of odontoblast differentiation.

claim: Control maxillary molars have three roots at two weeks of age.
source: In order to investigate whether mandibular and maxillary tooth furcations develop similarly, we also analyzed maxillary molars from two-week-old mice, which have three roots rather than the two of mandibular molars in controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G–1J).
evidence: Supported by microCT images in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G–1J.

claim: Maxillary molars were single-rooted with no furcation formation in Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl mice.
source: We found that maxillary molars were also single-rooted with no furcation formation in Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1K–1N), suggesting that the mechanisms regulating root patterning and furcation development are similar for maxillary and mandibular molars.
evidence: Supported by microCT images in Figure 2—figure supplement 1K–1N.

claim: The mechanisms regulating root patterning and furcation development are similar for maxillary and mandibular molars.
source: We found that maxillary molars were also single-rooted with no furcation formation in Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1K–1N), suggesting that the mechanisms regulating root patterning and furcation development are similar for maxillary and mandibular molars.
evidence: Inferred from the similar phenotypes observed in both maxillary and mandibular molars upon Ezh2 deletion.

claim: At PN 1 week, the epithelial diaphragm was not fused at the furcation region in control mice.
source: At PN 1 week, the epithelial diaphragm was not fused at the furcation region in control mice, as evidenced by a lack of continuous Krt14 staining in the apical region of the molar (Figure 3A–3B).
evidence: Supported by Krt14 immunofluorescence in Figures 3A-3B.

claim: One day later (PN 8 days), a fused epithelial diaphragm was detectable in control mice.
source: One day later, a fused epithelial diaphragm was detectable in control mice (Figure 3G–3H).
evidence: Supported by Krt14 immunofluorescence in Figures 3G-3H.

claim: Epithelial diaphragms were not detected in Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl mice at any time point.
source: In contrast, we did not detect epithelial diaphragms in Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl mice at any time point (Figure 3D–3E and J–K).
evidence: Supported by Krt14 immunofluorescence in Figures 3D-3E and J-K.

claim: Cell proliferation activity in the mesenchyme of the apical region was compromised in molars of Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl mice just prior to the time point at which epithelial diaphragm formation would normally be expected.
source: Moreover, cell proliferation activity in the mesenchyme of the apical region was compromised in molars of Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl mice just prior to the time point at which epithelial diaphragm formation would normally be expected (Figure 3C, F and I).
evidence: Supported by Ki67 staining and quantification shown in Figures 3C, F, and I.

claim: No apoptotic cells were detectable in the molars of control or Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl mice at PN 1 week or PN 3 weeks of age.
source: However, no apoptotic cells were detectable in the molars of control or Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl mice at PN 1 week or PN 3 weeks of age, indicating that loss of Ezh2 in the tooth mesenchyme has no impact on cell survival (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by TUNEL assay data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Loss of Ezh2 in the tooth mesenchyme has no impact on cell survival.
source: However, no apoptotic cells were detectable in the molars of control or Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl mice at PN 1 week or PN 3 weeks of age, indicating that loss of Ezh2 in the tooth mesenchyme has no impact on cell survival (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Inferred from the absence of apoptotic cells in TUNEL assays.

claim: At PN 2 weeks, alveolar bone was already formed between and underneath the molars of control mice.
source: At PN 2 weeks, alveolar bone was already formed between and underneath the molars of control mice.
evidence: Based on histological observations described in the text.

claim: Alveolar bone was undetectable in Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl mice until PN 4 weeks.
source: However, alveolar bone was undetectable in Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl mice until PN 4 weeks (Figure 4A–4B, D–E and G–J).
evidence: Supported by H&E staining in Figures 4A-4B, D-E, and G-J.

claim: Expression of PDL marker periostin was detectable in two-week-old control mice.
source: Similarly, expression of PDL marker periostin was detectable in two-week-old control mice, but its expression was undetectable in Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl mice (Figure 4C and F), indicating defective PDL formation due to loss of Ezh2 in the dental follicle.
evidence: Supported by periostin immunofluorescence in Figure 4C.

claim: Periostin expression was undetectable in Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl mice at two weeks of age.
source: Similarly, expression of PDL marker periostin was detectable in two-week-old control mice, but its expression was undetectable in Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl mice (Figure 4C and F), indicating defective PDL formation due to loss of Ezh2 in the dental follicle.
evidence: Supported by periostin immunofluorescence in Figure 4F.

claim: Loss of Ezh2 in the dental follicle causes defective PDL formation.
source: Similarly, expression of PDL marker periostin was detectable in two-week-old control mice, but its expression was undetectable in Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl mice (Figure 4C and F), indicating defective PDL formation due to loss of Ezh2 in the dental follicle.
evidence: Inferred from the absence of periostin expression, which is a PDL marker.

claim: Ezh2 in the dental mesenchyme is crucial for the development of alveolar bone and PDL.
source: Collectively, our studies show that Ezh2 in the dental mesenchyme is crucial for the development of alveolar bone and PDL.
evidence: Based on the observed defects in alveolar bone and PDL formation in Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl mice.

claim: At PN 2 weeks, the furcation was already formed in control molars.
source: At PN 2 weeks, the furcation was already formed in control molars, but it was not detectable in molars of Krt14-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl mice (Figure 5A–5J).
evidence: Supported by microCT images in Figures 5A-5E.

claim: The furcation was not detectable in molars of Krt14-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl mice at PN 2 weeks.
source: At PN 2 weeks, the furcation was already formed in control molars, but it was not detectable in molars of Krt14-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl mice (Figure 5A–5J).
evidence: Supported by microCT images in Figures 5F-5J.

claim: Alveolar bone formation was delayed in Krt14-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl mice at PN 2 weeks.
source: Interestingly, alveolar bone formation was delayed in Krt14-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl mice at PN 2 weeks (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–1B).
evidence: Supported by H&E staining in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–1B.

claim: By PN 3 weeks, the alveolar bone and molar root furcation had formed in Krt14-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl mice.
source: However, by PN 3 weeks, the alveolar bone and molar root furcation had formed in Krt14-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl mice (Figure 5K–5T and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–1F), indicating delayed furcation development due to loss of Ezh2 in the dental epithelium.
evidence: Supported by microCT images in Figures 5K-5T and H&E staining in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–1F.

claim: Loss of Ezh2 in the dental epithelium causes delayed furcation development.
source: However, by PN 3 weeks, the alveolar bone and molar root furcation had formed in Krt14-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl mice (Figure 5K–5T and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–1F), indicating delayed furcation development due to loss of Ezh2 in the dental epithelium.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that furcation eventually forms but at a later time point.

claim: There were no distinguishable differences between the tooth roots of Dmp1-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl and control mice at PN 3 weeks.
source: We found no distinguishable differences between the tooth roots of Dmp1-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl and control mice at PN 3 weeks, based on CT images and H&E staining (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by microCT images and H&E staining in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Alveolar bone and PDL formation were normal in Dmp1-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl mice when compared to control samples.
source: Alveolar bone and PDL formation were also normal in Dmp1-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl mice when compared to control samples.
evidence: Based on histological observations described in the text.

claim: Ezh2 in odontoblasts is not required for root patterning and furcation development.
source: Collectively, our results indicate that Ezh2 in odontoblasts is not required for root patterning and furcation development.
evidence: Inferred from the normal root development observed in Dmp1-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl mice.

claim: Arid1a is part of the SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complex.
source: Arid1a is part of the SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complex and has an antagonistic relationship with Ezh2 of the PRC2 complex in cancer development (Bitler et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2018).
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge and cited references.

claim: Arid1a has an antagonistic relationship with Ezh2 of the PRC2 complex in cancer development.
source: Arid1a is part of the SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complex and has an antagonistic relationship with Ezh2 of the PRC2 complex in cancer development (Bitler et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by cited references to previous studies.

claim: Arid1a has a similar expression pattern to that of Ezh2 during root development.
source: Arid1a has a similar expression pattern to that of Ezh2 during root development.
evidence: Based on observations described in the text.

claim: The expression of Arid1a was not affected in the molars of Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl mice.
source: Interestingly, it appears that the expression of Arid1a was not affected in the molars of Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), indicating Arid1a is not a downstream target of Ezh2.
evidence: Supported by Arid1a immunofluorescence in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Arid1a is not a downstream target of Ezh2.
source: Interestingly, it appears that the expression of Arid1a was not affected in the molars of Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), indicating Arid1a is not a downstream target of Ezh2.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Arid1a expression is unchanged in Ezh2 mutants.

claim: The antagonism between Ezh2 and Arid1a may occur on the functional level.
source: However, previous studies have shown that the antagonism between Ezh2 and Arid1a may occur on the functional level (Bitler et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by cited reference to previous study.

claim: The abnormal root patterning and furcation development seen in Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl mice were completely rescued in Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl;Arid1afl/+ molars.
source: Indeed, the abnormal root patterning and furcation development seen in Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl mice were completely rescued in Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl;Arid1afl/+ molars, based on microCT images (Figure 6A–6L), indicating that Arid1a and Ezh2 may work antagonistically to control furcation development.
evidence: Supported by microCT images in Figures 6A-6L showing rescue of furcation phenotype.

claim: Arid1a and Ezh2 may work antagonistically to control furcation development.
source: Indeed, the abnormal root patterning and furcation development seen in Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl mice were completely rescued in Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl;Arid1afl/+ molars, based on microCT images (Figure 6A–6L), indicating that Arid1a and Ezh2 may work antagonistically to control furcation development.
evidence: Inferred from the genetic rescue experiment showing that reducing Arid1a dosage rescues Ezh2 loss phenotype.

claim: Root furcations in Osr2-Cre;Arid1afl/+ mice were identical to those of control mice.
source: To examine whether monoallelic deletion of Arid1a affects furcation development, we generated Osr2-Cre;Arid1afl/+ mice and found that their root furcations were identical to those of control mice (n = 4), suggesting that haploinsufficiency of Arid1a did not affect root patterning or development (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by microCT images in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Haploinsufficiency of Arid1a did not affect root patterning or development.
source: To examine whether monoallelic deletion of Arid1a affects furcation development, we generated Osr2-Cre;Arid1afl/+ mice and found that their root furcations were identical to those of control mice (n = 4), suggesting that haploinsufficiency of Arid1a did not affect root patterning or development (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Osr2-Cre;Arid1afl/+ mice have normal furcations.

claim: Alveolar bone and PDL development was rescued in Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl;Arid1afl/+ mice at PN 3 weeks.
source: We also analyzed alveolar bone and PDL development at PN 3 weeks and found that there was no difference between the molars of Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl;Arid1afl/+ and control mice, suggesting that alveolar bone and PDL devlopment was also rescued in Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl;Arid1afl/+ mice (Figure 6).
evidence: Based on histological observations and images in Figure 6.

claim: More genes were upregulated than downregulated in Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl molars.
source: We found that more genes were upregulated than downregulated in Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl molars (Figure 7A), consistent with the gene repression function of Ezh2.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq heatmap in Figure 7A.

claim: The upregulation of more genes than downregulated genes in Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl molars is consistent with the gene repression function of Ezh2.
source: We found that more genes were upregulated than downregulated in Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl molars (Figure 7A), consistent with the gene repression function of Ezh2.
evidence: Based on established knowledge that Ezh2 functions as a transcriptional repressor.

claim: Patterning genes such as Hox family members and Hand2 were highly enriched and among the top twenty upregulated genes in Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl molars.
source: Patterning genes such as Hox family members and Hand2 were highly enriched and among the top twenty upregulated genes, indicating their potential role in root furcation development.
evidence: Based on RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: Hox family members and Hand2 have a potential role in root furcation development.
source: Patterning genes such as Hox family members and Hand2 were highly enriched and among the top twenty upregulated genes, indicating their potential role in root furcation development.
evidence: Inferred from their upregulation in the Ezh2 mutant with furcation defects.

claim: Cdkn2a was upregulated in the root-forming dental mesenchyme in Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl molars.
source: Interestingly, we found that Cdkn2a, a cell cycle inhibitor, was also upregulated in the root-forming dental mesenchyme in Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl molars, consistent with the observed reduction in cell proliferation activity.
evidence: Based on RNA-seq data showing Cdkn2a upregulation.

claim: Cdkn2a is a cell cycle inhibitor.
source: Interestingly, we found that Cdkn2a, a cell cycle inhibitor, was also upregulated in the root-forming dental mesenchyme in Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl molars, consistent with the observed reduction in cell proliferation activity.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about Cdkn2a function.

claim: The upregulation of Cdkn2a in Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl molars is consistent with the observed reduction in cell proliferation activity.
source: Interestingly, we found that Cdkn2a, a cell cycle inhibitor, was also upregulated in the root-forming dental mesenchyme in Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl molars, consistent with the observed reduction in cell proliferation activity.
evidence: Logical inference connecting Cdkn2a's known function as a cell cycle inhibitor with the observed proliferation defect.

claim: Cdkn2a expression was upregulated in Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl mice compared to controls.
source: In order to test our hypothesis, we first examined the expression of Cdkn2a in the molar root-forming region and found that it was upregulated in Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl mice (Figure 7B and D)
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data in Figures 7B and D.

claim: The level of Cdkn2a expression was restored to the control level in Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl;Arid1afl/+ molars.
source: whereas the level of Cdkn2a expression was restored to the level in control samples in Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl;Arid1afl/+ molars (Figure 7F).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data in Figure 7F.

claim: Cell proliferation was restored in Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl;Arid1afl/+ molars.
source: Based on this finding, we further examined cell proliferation activity in the root-forming region and found that proliferation was also restored in Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl;Arid1afl/+ molars (Figure 7C, E, G and H).
evidence: Supported by Ki67 staining and quantification in Figures 7C, E, G, and H.

claim: Hox genes and Cdkn2a are in the H3K27Me3 binding sites in root mesenchyme of control molars.
source: Furthermore we performed the CHIP sequencing of H3K27Me3 in root mesenchyme of the control molars. Interestingly, our data have shown that the Hox genes and Cdkn2a are in the H3K27Me3 binding sites (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), which is consistent with our RNA sequencing data.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The antagonistic interaction between Ezh2 and Arid1a controls Cdkn2a expression in regulating cell proliferation during root patterning and furcation development.
source: Collectively, our data highlight a critical role for the antagnistic interaction between Ezh2 and Arid1a in controlling Cdkn2a expression in regulating cell proliferation during root patterning and furcation development.
evidence: Based on the combined genetic, expression, and proliferation data showing rescue of all phenotypes.

claim: Epithelial-mesenchymal interaction is crucial for organ patterning and morphogenesis.
source: Epithelial-mesenchymal interaction is crucial for organ patterning and morphogenesis.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: During the formation of branched organs, the mesenchyme can instruct the epithelium to form branching patterns.
source: During the formation of branched organs, the mesenchyme can instruct the epithelium to form branching patterns.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Various types of signaling in the mesenchyme, including WNT, hedgehog (HH) and bone morphogenetic protein (BMP), play important roles in regulating branch patterning and morphogenesis in the salivary gland, kidney and lung.
source: For example, various types of signaling in the mesenchyme, including WNT, hedgehog (HH) and bone morphogenetic protein (BMP), play important roles in regulating branch patterning and morphogenesis in the salivary gland, kidney and lung (Lu and Werb, 2008).
evidence: Supported by cited reference to previous study.

claim: Epithelial-mesenchymal interaction is crucial for tooth root patterning and morphogenesis.
source: Similarly, epithelial-mesenchymal interaction is also crucial for tooth root patterning and morphogenesis.
evidence: Based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: The pattern of HERS growth may correlate with the number, length, and shape of roots.
source: Previous studies have suggested that the pattern of HERS growth may correlate with the number, length, and shape of roots (Kumakami-Sakano et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by cited reference to previous study.

claim: HERS provides instructive signals that contribute to the induction of dental mesenchyme differentiation.
source: Furthermore, HERS provides instructive signals that contribute to the induction of dental mesenchyme differentiation, suggesting that it functions as a signaling center to guide root formation (Huang et al., 2009; Li et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by cited references to previous studies.

claim: HERS functions as a signaling center to guide root formation.
source: Furthermore, HERS provides instructive signals that contribute to the induction of dental mesenchyme differentiation, suggesting that it functions as a signaling center to guide root formation (Huang et al., 2009; Li et al., 2017).
evidence: Inferred from previous studies cited.

claim: HERS-derived TGFβ/BMP signaling regulates root dentin formation through Nfic expression in the dental mesenchyme.
source: For example, HERS-derived TGFβ/BMP signaling regulates root dentin formation through Nfic expression in the dental mesenchyme (Huang et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by cited reference to previous study.

claim: The pattern of the cervical epithelial diaphragm may guide furcation formation.
source: Previous studies have suggested that the pattern of the cervical epithelial diaphragm may guide furcation formation, and signals from HERS may have a critical impact on determination of the root number.
evidence: Based on previous studies in the field.

claim: Signals from HERS may have a critical impact on determination of the root number.
source: Previous studies have suggested that the pattern of the cervical epithelial diaphragm may guide furcation formation, and signals from HERS may have a critical impact on determination of the root number.
evidence: Based on previous studies in the field.

claim: The Eda pathway is specifically active in HERS in mouse molars.
source: For instance, the Eda pathway is specifically active in HERS in mouse molars.
evidence: Based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Cell proliferation activity is altered in the dental mesenchyme in Eda mutant molars with delayed furcation formation.
source: Cell proliferation activity is altered in the dental mesenchyme in Eda mutant molars with delayed furcation formation, suggesting that epithelial-derived signals may regulate furcation development through epithelial-mesenchymal interaction (Fons Romero et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by cited reference to previous study.

claim: Epithelial-derived signals may regulate furcation development through epithelial-mesenchymal interaction.
source: Cell proliferation activity is altered in the dental mesenchyme in Eda mutant molars with delayed furcation formation, suggesting that epithelial-derived signals may regulate furcation development through epithelial-mesenchymal interaction (Fons Romero et al., 2017).
evidence: Inferred from observations in Eda mutants as cited.

claim: The directionality of HERS growth may be regulated by differential proliferation of mesenchymal cells in furcation-forming and root-forming regions.
source: The directionality of HERS growth may be regulated by differential proliferation of mesenchymal cells in furcation-forming and root-forming regions, which in turn determines root number (Sohn et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by cited reference to previous study.

claim: Differential proliferation of mesenchymal cells in furcation-forming and root-forming regions determines root number.
source: The directionality of HERS growth may be regulated by differential proliferation of mesenchymal cells in furcation-forming and root-forming regions, which in turn determines root number (Sohn et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by cited reference to previous study.

claim: Loss of Ezh2 in the tooth mesenchyme transformed multi-rooted molars into single-rooted ones in the mouse.
source: In this study, we found that loss of Ezh2 in the tooth mesenchyme transformed multi-rooted molars into single-rooted ones in the mouse, suggesting the significance of the dental mesenchyme in regulating root pattern and furcation development.
evidence: Based on the experimental results presented in the study.

claim: The dental mesenchyme is significant in regulating root pattern and furcation development.
source: In this study, we found that loss of Ezh2 in the tooth mesenchyme transformed multi-rooted molars into single-rooted ones in the mouse, suggesting the significance of the dental mesenchyme in regulating root pattern and furcation development.
evidence: Inferred from the dramatic phenotype observed upon mesenchymal Ezh2 deletion.

claim: Loss of Ezh2 in the dental epithelium resulted in delayed furcation development without affecting root patterning.
source: In contrast, loss of Ezh2 in the dental epithelium resulted in delayed furcation development without affecting root patterning.
evidence: Based on the experimental results with Krt14-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl mice.

claim: Signals from the mesenchyme, rather than the epithelium, are the driving force behind tooth patterning.
source: These data suggest that signals from the mesenchyme, rather than the epithelium, are the driving force behind tooth patterning.
evidence: Inferred from comparing the phenotypes of mesenchymal vs. epithelial Ezh2 deletion.

claim: Loss of Ezh2 in the dental mesenchyme affects the growth of HERS through mesenchymal-epithelial interaction.
source: It is possible that loss of Ezh2 in the dental mesenchyme affects the growth of HERS through mesenchymal-epithelial interaction.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the mechanism underlying the observed phenotype.

claim: The epithelial diaphragm fails to fuse at the future furcation site in Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl mice.
source: This is highlighted by the phenotype in which the epithelial diaphragm fails to fuse at the future furcation site in Osr2-Cre;Ezh2fl/fl mice.
evidence: Based on the experimental observations presented earlier in the study.

claim: Root defects are mainly related to signaling alterations in the mesenchyme rather than the epithelium.
source: Previous studies have also highlighted that root defects are mainly related to signaling alterations in the mesenchyme rather than the epithelium (Li et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by cited reference to previous study.

claim: In humans, mutations adversely affecting the dental mesenchyme are closely associated with tooth root defects.
source: Moreover, in humans, mutations adversely affecting the dental mesenchyme are closely associated with tooth root defects.
evidence: Based on established clinical knowledge.

claim: Dentinogenesis imperfecta type I is attributed to mutations in COL1A1 and COL1A2.
source: For example, dentinogenesis imperfecta type I (attributed to mutations in COL1A1 and COL1A2) and dentinogenesis imperfecta type II (caused by mutations in DSPP) both involve root defects.
evidence: Based on established clinical knowledge.

claim: Dentinogenesis imperfecta type II is caused by mutations in DSPP.
